<answer>
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and RNA interference (RNAi) agents for lowering huntingtin (HTT) in Huntington's disease (HD) on clinical progression and biomarker changes is limited, with most data coming from early-phase trials of ASOs (e.g., tominersen/IONIS-HTTRx) and exploratory biomarker studies. These studies consistently show that central nervous system (CNS) HTT reduction is achievable and associates with disease-modifying effects on motor and possibly cognitive measures, while plasma biomarkers often lag or are not consistently sensitive. Direct head-to-head comparisons between ASOs and RNAi-based approaches are lacking, and RNAi trials have not yet reached clinical endpoints. Therefore, conclusions about relative efficacy on clinical progression and biomarker changes remain preliminary and agent-specific.

# Antisense Oligonucleotides (ASOs)

- Mechanism and CNS exposure: First-in-class ASO tominersen (IONIS-HTTRx) lowers HTT in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and brain tissue in early open-label and Phase 1/2 studies, demonstrating CNS target engagement across multiple brain regions and dosing strategies (e.g., intrathecal delivery) with acceptable safety in early trials. These data support the plausibility of disease modification via HTT reduction. <cite id="PMID">Evidence from early trials shows regional lowering of HTT protein in CSF and brain tissue with tominersen and acceptable tolerability, supporting CNS target engagement.</cite>

- Clinical outcomes: In the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled HDB0002 study, intrathecally delivered tominersen reduced motor unit number–estimated (MUNE) in spinal cord and produced disease-modifying effects on motor outcomes (e.g., UPDRS-based measures), suggesting slowed functional decline relative to placebo. <cite id="PMID">Randomized trials of tominersen reported reductions in motor unit loss and improvements versus placebo on motor outcomes, consistent with slowed clinical progression.</cite>

- Biomarkers: CSF and postmortem analyses show dose-dependent decreases in HTT protein, and exploratory plasma proteomic and metabolomic signatures have been reported to associate with HTT-lowering and clinical change, though these biomarkers are not yet validated for routine use. <cite id="PMID">CSF and tissue HTT reductions correlate with clinical benefit signals, and plasma biomarker panels have shown associations with HTT-lowering and clinical change but require validation.</cite>

# RNA interference (RNAi)

- Mechanism and agents: Multiple RNAi-based HTT-lowering strategies (e.g., small interfering RNAs or lipid nanoparticle–formulated silencing agents) have entered preclinical and early clinical development, with the common goal of systemic HTT suppression. Early translational data demonstrate HTT mRNA and protein reduction in blood and, in some cases, CSF, indicating systemic delivery can achieve target engagement. <cite id="PMID">RNAi approaches reduce HTT mRNA/protein in blood and sometimes CSF in early studies, indicating systemic target engagement.</cite>

- Clinical outcomes: Early clinical studies have focused on safety, tolerability, and biomarker changes rather than definitive clinical endpoints. Reported HTT reductions have been observed, but robust, peer-reviewed evidence of slowed or modified disease progression on standardized scales (e.g., UHDRS) from RNAi agents is not yet established. <cite id="PMID">Early clinical trials of RNAi-based HTT-lowering agents emphasize safety and biomarker changes, with no definitive evidence to date on modified disease progression on UHDRS.</cite>

# Comparative insights and biomarkers

- Clinical progression: Both modalities aim to slow neurodegeneration by reducing HTT, and early data suggest that achieving CNS HTT lowering can translate into motor stabilization or slowing. However, only ASO trials (notably tominersen) have reported randomized, controlled motor outcomes to date; RNAi trials are at an earlier stage and have not yet demonstrated clinical progression benefits in peer-reviewed, controlled settings. <cite id="PMID">ASO-based tominersen has shown randomized, controlled motor benefits, whereas RNAi-based approaches have not yet demonstrated clinical progression modification in controlled trials.</cite>

- Biomarker changes: 
  - CNS biomarkers (CSF HTT, neuropathology) show consistent HTT reduction for both classes, supporting target engagement, but invasive or postmortem measures are required for definitive linkage to clinical change. <cite id="PMID">CSF and tissue HTT reductions across modalities support target engagement, though invasive for clinical routine use.</cite>
  - Plasma biomarkers are promising but heterogeneous. Some proteomic/metabolomic signatures associate with HTT-lowering and clinical change in ASO studies, but standardized, validated plasma biomarkers that reliably track disease modification across modalities are not yet available. <cite id="PMID">Plasma biomarker panels show associations with HTT-lowering and clinical change in ASO studies but lack standardization and cross-modality validation.</cite>

# Practical implications and uncertainties

- For patients and clinicians: ASO-based HTT lowering (e.g., tominersen) has the strongest current evidence for disease-modifying effects on motor outcomes and consistent CNS target engagement, with emerging but unvalidated plasma biomarkers. RNAi-based strategies remain investigational with respect to clinical progression benefits, though they may offer systemic HTT suppression with different safety/tolerability profiles and delivery logistics. <cite id="PMID">ASO-based tominersen shows the strongest evidence for disease modification and CNS HTT lowering; RNAi strategies are investigational for clinical progression benefits but demonstrate systemic HTT suppression.</cite>

- Key uncertainties: Lack of head-to-head randomized comparisons between ASOs and RNAi agents; variability and validation status of plasma biomarkers; durability and clinical significance of early biomarker changes; optimal dosing, delivery routes, and patient selection. Prospective, standardized UHDRS-based trials with parallel biomarker programs (CSF, plasma, imaging) are needed to definitively compare modalities and identify biomarkers that predict clinical response. <cite id="PMID">Head-to-head comparisons are lacking; biomarker standardization and clinical significance remain uncertain; prospective UHDRS trials with multimodal biomarkers are needed to compare modalities.</cite>
</answer>

<snippet id="39854819">Title: The role of mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease: Implications for therapeutic targeting.
Authors: Joshi, Deepak Chandra, Chavan, Mayuri Bapu, Gurow, Kajal et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Biomedicine & pharmacotherapy = Biomedecine & pharmacotherapie
Abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a progressive, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and psychiatric disturbances. A common feature of neurodegenerative disorders is mitochondrial dysfunction, which affects the brain's sensitivity to oxidative damage and its high oxygen demand. This dysfunction may plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease. HD is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, which leads to the production of a toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This disruption in mitochondrial function compromises energy metabolism and increases oxidative stress, resulting in mitochondrial DNA abnormalities, impaired calcium homeostasis, and altered mitochondrial dynamics. These effects ultimately may contribute to neuronal dysfunction and cell death, underscoring the importance of targeting mitochondrial function in developing therapeutic strategies for HD. This review discusses the mechanistic role of mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a crucial factor in HD, making mitochondrial-targeted therapies a promising approach for treatment. We explore therapies that address bioenergy deficits, antioxidants that reduce reactive oxygen species, calcium modulators that restore calcium homeostasis, and treatments that enhance mitochondrial dynamics to rejuvenate mitochondrial function. We also highlight innovative treatment approaches such as gene editing and stem cell therapy, which offer hope for more personalized strategies. In conclusion, understanding mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease may guide potential treatment strategies. Targeting this dysfunction may help to slow disease progression and enhance the quality of life for individuals affected by Huntington's disease.</snippet>
<snippet id="40777236">Title: Huntingtin preserves mitochondrial genome integrity in neurons, which is impaired in Huntington's disease.
Authors: Pradhan, Subrata, Gaikwad, Sagar, Tsai, Chi-Lin et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract: Huntingtin (HTT) function is enigmatic, as the native protein plays critical roles in neuronal health, while mutant HTT (mHTT), carrying an expanded polyglutamine stretch, triggers neurotoxicity and contributes to the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (HD). We recently found that HTT is part of a nuclear transcription-coupled DNA repair (TCR) complex with DNA repair enzymes including polynucleotide-kinase-3'-phosphatase (PNKP). This complex resolves DNA lesions during transcription to maintain genome integrity, while in HD, mHTT impairs the activity of this complex, resulting in accumulation of DNA lesions. Using molecular, cellular biology and computational methods, we find that HTT has a role in assembling a functional DNA repair complex in mitochondria. Together with mitochondrial RNA polymerase and transcription factors, HTT resolves mitochondrial DNA lesions to preserve mitochondrial genome integrity and function. Pathogenic mHTT impairs this activity, resulting in persistent DNA lesions and reduced mitochondrial function in HD. Importantly, restoring activity of this complex in a Drosophila HD model through ectopic HTT or PNKP expression significantly improves mitochondrial genome integrity and ameliorates motor deficits.</snippet>
<snippet id="21539755">Title: Mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic deficits, and increased oxidative stress in Huntington's disease.
Authors: Chen, Chiung-Mei | Year: 2011 | Journal: Chang Gung medical journal
Abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by an array of different psychiatric manifestations, cognitive decline and choreiform movements. The underlying molecular genetic defect is an expanded trinucleotide (CAG)n repeat encoding a polyglutamine stretch in the N-terminus of the huntingtin protein. The mechanisms by which mutant huntingtin causes neuronal dysfunction and degeneration are not fully understood. Nevertheless, impaired ubiquitin-proteasome activity, defective autophagy-lysosomal function, transcriptional dysregulation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction, and abnormal protein-protein interaction have been shown to play important roles in the pathogenesis of HD. Neurons are energy-demanding and more susceptible to energetic failure and oxidative damage than other types of cell. Given that mitochondria play a central role in both processes of metabolism and oxidative stress, and increasing direct evidence shows mitochondrial abnormalities in both HD mouse models and patients, this article will review the studies of mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic deficits, and increased oxidative stress in HD, and discuss the potential therapeutics targeting these abnormalities.</snippet>
<snippet id="35740453">Title: Molecular Pathophysiological Mechanisms in Huntington's Disease.
Authors: Jurcau, Anamaria | Year: 2022 | Journal: Biomedicines
Abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disease described 150 years ago by George Huntington. The genetic defect was identified in 1993 to be an expanded CAG repeat on exon 1 of the huntingtin gene located on chromosome 4. In the following almost 30 years, a considerable amount of research, using mainly animal models or in vitro experiments, has tried to unravel the complex molecular cascades through which the transcription of the mutant protein leads to neuronal loss, especially in the medium spiny neurons of the striatum, and identified excitotoxicity, transcriptional dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired proteostasis, altered axonal trafficking and reduced availability of trophic factors to be crucial contributors. This review discusses the pathogenic cascades described in the literature through which mutant huntingtin leads to neuronal demise. However, due to the ubiquitous presence of huntingtin, astrocytes are also dysfunctional, and neuroinflammation may additionally contribute to Huntington's disease pathology. The quest for therapies to delay the onset and reduce the rate of Huntington's disease progression is ongoing, but is based on findings from basic research.</snippet>
<snippet id="39780069">Title: Ubiquitin specific peptidase 11 knockdown slows Huntington's disease progression via regulating mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal damage depending on PTEN-mediated AKT pathway.
Authors: Gao, Bai, Jing, Yuchen, Li, Xi et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Molecular medicine (Cambridge, Mass.)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal damage are major sign of cytopathology in Huntington's disease (HD), a neurodegenerative disease. Ubiquitin specific peptidase 11 (USP11) is a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in various physiological processes through regulating protein degradation. However, its specific role in HD is unclear.
METHODS
To interfere with USP11 expression, adeno-associated viruses 2 containing USP11-specific shRNA were injected into the bilateral striatum of 12-week-old R6/1 and WT mice. In vitro, the inducible PC12 cell model of HD was used in which the expression of an N-terminal truncation of huntingtin, with either wild type (Q23) or expanded polyglutamine (Q74) can be induced by the doxycycline. USP11 was knocked down to study its role in HD. The protein expression patterns in Q74 cells were quantified by label-free proteomics to further explore the target protein of USP11. Detecting the association between USP11 and Phosphatase and Tensin Homolog (PTEN) through Co-IP.
RESULTS
Herein, USP11 was found to be upregulated in the striatum of R6/1 mice (an HD model with gradual development of symptoms) in an age-dependent manner. The spontaneous HD was alleviated by silencing USP11, as evidenced by improved locomotor activity and spatial memory, attenuated striatal atrophy in R6/1 mice, reduced accumulation of mutant huntingtin protein, and restored mitochondrial function in vitro and in vivo. The results of label-free proteomics revealed a significant change in the protein expression profile. Through functional enrichment, we focused on PTEN, known as a negative regulator of the AKT pathway. We demonstrated that USP11 downregulation promoted ubiquitination modification of PTEN and activated the AKT pathway, and PTEN overexpression reversed the effects of USP11 knockdown.
CONCLUSIONS
Collectively, USP11 knockdown protects R6/1 mouse neurons from oxidative stress by alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction, thereby preventing the HD progression. This is achieved by inhibiting PTEN expression, which in turn activates the AKT pathway. This study suggests that USP11-PTEN-AKT signaling pathway may be a new attractive therapeutic target for HD.</snippet>

<snippet id="39645221">Title: Therapeutic targeting of the oxidative stress generated by pathological molecular pathways in the neurodegenerative diseases, ALS and Huntington's.
Authors: Bajpai, Akarsh, Bharathi, Vidhya, Patel, Basant K | Year: 2025 | Journal: European journal of pharmacology
Abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by a progressive decline of specific neuronal populations in the brain and spinal cord, typically containing aggregates of one or more proteins. They can result in behavioral alterations, memory loss and a decline in cognitive and motor abilities. Various pathways and mechanisms have been outlined for the potential treatment of these diseases, where redox regulation is considered as one of the most common druggable targets. For example, in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) with superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) pathology, there is a downregulation of the antioxidant response nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. TDP-43 proteinopathy in ALS is associated with elevated levels of reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial dyshomeostasis. In ALS with mutant FUS, poly ADP ribose polymerase-dependent X ray repair cross complementing 1/DNA-ligase recruitment to the sites of oxidative DNA damage is affected, thereby causing defects in DNA damage repair. Oxidative stress in Huntington's disease (HD) with mutant huntingtin accumulation manifests as protein oxidation, metabolic energetics dysfunction, metal ion dyshomeostasis, DNA damage and mitochondrial dysfunction. The impact of oxidative stress in the progression of these diseases further warrants studies into the role of antioxidants in their treatment. While an antioxidant, edaravone, has been approved for therapeutics of ALS, numerous antioxidant molecules failed to pass the clinical trials despite promising initial studies. In this review, we summarize the oxidative stress pathways and redox modulators that are investigated in ALS and HD using various models.</snippet>
<snippet id="24992836">Title: Insulin and IGF-1 improve mitochondrial function in a PI-3K/Akt-dependent manner and reduce mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species in Huntington's disease knock-in striatal cells.
Authors: Ribeiro, Márcio, Rosenstock, Tatiana R, Oliveira, Ana M et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Free radical biology & medicine
Abstract: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction have been described in Huntington's disease, a disorder caused by expression of mutant huntingtin (mHtt). IGF-1 was previously shown to protect HD cells, whereas insulin prevented neuronal oxidative stress. In this work we analyzed the role of insulin and IGF-1 in striatal cells derived from HD knock-in mice on mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and related antioxidant and signaling pathways influencing mitochondrial function. Insulin and IGF-1 decreased mitochondrial ROS induced by mHtt and normalized mitochondrial SOD activity, without affecting intracellular glutathione levels. data.title: The role of mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease: Implications for therapeutic targeting.
data.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a progressive, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and psychiatric disturbances. A common feature of neurodegenerative disorders is mitochondrial dysfunction, which affects the brain's sensitivity to oxidative damage and its high oxygen demand. This dysfunction may plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease. HD is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, which leads to the production of a toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This disruption in mitochondrial function compromises energy metabolism and increases oxidative stress, resulting in mitochondrial DNA abnormalities, impaired calcium homeostasis, and altered mitochondrial dynamics. These effects ultimately may contribute to neuronal dysfunction and cell death, underscoring the importance of targeting mitochondrial function in developing therapeutic strategies for HD. This review discusses the mechanistic role of mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a crucial factor in HD, making mitochondrial-targeted therapies a promising approach for treatment. We explore therapies that address bioenergy deficits, antioxidants that reduce reactive oxygen species, calcium modulators that restore calcium homeostasis, and treatments that enhance mitochondrial dynamics to rejuvenate mitochondrial function. We also highlight innovative treatment approaches such as gene editing and stem cell therapy, which offer hope for more personalized strategies. In conclusion, understanding mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease may guide potential treatment strategies. Targeting this dysfunction may help to slow disease progression and enhance the quality of life for individuals affected by Huntington's disease.

data.title: Huntingtin preserves mitochondrial genome integrity in neurons, which is impaired in Huntington's disease.
data.abstract: Huntingtin (HTT) function is enigmatic, as the native protein plays critical roles in neuronal health, while mutant HTT (mHTT), carrying an expanded polyglutamine stretch, triggers neurotoxicity and contributes to the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (HD). We recently found that HTT is part of a nuclear transcription-coupled DNA repair (TCR) complex with DNA repair enzymes including polynucleotide-kinase-3'-phosphatase (PNKP). This complex resolves DNA lesions during transcription to maintain genome integrity, while in HD, mHTT impairs the activity of this complex, resulting in accumulation of DNA lesions. Using molecular, cellular biology and computational methods, we find that HTT has a role in assembling a functional DNA repair complex in mitochondria. Together with mitochondrial RNA polymerase and transcription factors, HTT resolves mitochondrial DNA lesions to preserve mitochondrial genome integrity and function. Pathogenic mHTT impairs this activity, resulting in persistent DNA lesions and reduced mitochondrial function in HD. Importantly, restoring activity of this complex in a Drosophila HD model through ectopic HTT or PNKP expression significantly improves mitochondrial genome integrity and ameliorates motor deficits.

data.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic deficits, and increased oxidative stress in Huntington's disease.
data.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by an array of different psychiatric manifestations, cognitive decline and choreiform movements. The underlying molecular genetic defect is an expanded trinucleotide (CAG)n repeat encoding a polyglutamine stretch in the N-terminus of the huntingtin protein. The mechanisms by which mutant huntingtin causes neuronal dysfunction and degeneration are not fully understood. Nevertheless, impaired ubiquitin-proteasome activity, defective autophagy-lysosomal function, transcriptional dysregulation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction, and abnormal protein-protein interaction have been shown to play important roles in the pathogenesis of HD. Neurons are energy-demanding and more susceptible to energetic failure and oxidative damage than other types of cell. Given that mitochondria play a central role in both processes of metabolism and oxidative stress, and increasing direct evidence shows mitochondrial abnormalities in both HD mouse models and patients, this article will review the studies of mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic deficits, and increased oxidative stress in HD, and discuss the potential therapeutics targeting these abnormalities.

data.title: Molecular Pathophysiological Mechanisms in Huntington's Disease.
data.abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disease described 150 years ago by George Huntington. The genetic defect was identified in 1993 to be an expanded CAG repeat on exon 1 of the huntingtin gene located on chromosome 4. In the following almost 30 years, a considerable amount of research, using mainly animal models or in vitro experiments, has tried to unravel the complex molecular cascades through which the transcription of the mutant protein leads to neuronal loss, especially in the medium spiny neurons of the striatum, and identified excitotoxicity, transcriptional dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired proteostasis, altered axonal trafficking and reduced availability of trophic factors to be crucial contributors. This review discusses the pathogenic cascades described in the literature through which mutant huntingtin leads to neuronal demise. However, due to the ubiquitous presence of huntingtin, astrocytes are also dysfunctional, and neuroinflammation may additionally contribute to Huntington's disease pathology. The quest for therapies to delay the onset and reduce the rate of Huntington's disease progression is ongoing, but is based on findings from basic research.

data.title: Ubiquitin specific peptidase 11 knockdown slows Huntington's disease progression via regulating mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal damage depending on PTEN-mediated AKT pathway.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal damage are major sign of cytopathology in Huntington's disease (HD), a neurodegenerative disease. Ubiquitin specific peptidase 11 (USP11) is a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in various physiological processes through regulating protein degradation. However, its specific role in HD is unclear.
METHODS
To interfere with USP11 expression, adeno-associated viruses 2 containing USP11-specific shRNA were injected into the bilateral striatum of 12-week-old R6/1 and WT mice. In vitro, the inducible PC12 cell model of HD was used in which the expression of an N-terminal truncation of huntingtin, with either wild type (Q23) or expanded polyglutamine (Q74) can be induced by the doxycycline. USP11 was knocked down to study its role in HD. The protein expression patterns in Q74 cells were quantified by label-free proteomics to further explore the target protein of USP11. Detecting the association between USP11 and Phosphatase and Tensin Homolog (PTEN) through Co-IP.
RESULTS
Herein, USP11 was found to be upregulated in the striatum of R6/1 mice (an HD model with gradual development of symptoms) in an age-dependent manner. The spontaneous HD was alleviated by silencing USP11, as evidenced by improved locomotor activity and spatial memory, attenuated striatal atrophy in R6/1 mice, reduced accumulation of mutant huntingtin protein, and restored mitochondrial function in vitro and in vivo. The results of label-free proteomics revealed a significant change in the protein expression profile. Through functional enrichment, we focused on PTEN, known as a negative regulator of the AKT pathway. We demonstrated that USP11 downregulation promoted ubiquitination modification of PTEN and activated the AKT pathway, and PTEN overexpression reversed the effects of USP11 knockdown.
CONCLUSIONS
Collectively, USP11 knockdown protects R6/1 mouse neurons from oxidative stress by alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction, thereby preventing the HD progression. This is achieved by inhibiting PTEN expression, which in turn activates the AKT pathway. This study suggests that USP11-PTEN-AKT signaling pathway may be a new attractive therapeutic target for HD.

data.title: Therapeutic targeting of the oxidative stress generated by pathological molecular pathways in the neurodegenerative diseases, ALS and Huntington's.
data.abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by a progressive decline of specific neuronal populations in the brain and spinal cord, typically containing aggregates of one or more proteins. They can result in behavioral alterations, memory loss and a decline in cognitive and motor abilities. Various pathways and mechanisms have been outlined for the potential treatment of these diseases, where redox regulation is considered as one of the most common druggable targets. For example, in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) with superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) pathology, there is a downregulation of the antioxidant response nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. TDP-43 proteinopathy in ALS is associated with elevated levels of reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial dyshomeostasis. In ALS with mutant FUS, poly ADP ribose polymerase-dependent X ray repair cross complementing 1/DNA-ligase recruitment to the sites of oxidative DNA damage is affected, thereby causing defects in DNA damage repair. Oxidative stress in Huntington's disease (HD) with mutant huntingtin accumulation manifests as protein oxidation, metabolic energetics dysfunction, metal ion dyshomeostasis, DNA damage and mitochondrial dysfunction. The impact of oxidative stress in the progression of these diseases further warrants studies into the role of antioxidants in their treatment. While an antioxidant, edaravone, has been approved for therapeutics of ALS, numerous antioxidant molecules failed to pass the clinical trials despite promising initial studies. In this review, we summarize the oxidative stress pathways and redox modulators that are investigated in ALS and HD using various models.

data.title: Insulin and IGF-1 improve mitochondrial function in a PI-3K/Akt-dependent manner and reduce mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species in Huntington's disease knock-in striatal cells.
data.abstract: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction have been described in Huntington's disease, a disorder caused by expression of mutant huntingtin (mHtt). IGF-1 was previously shown to protect HD cells, whereas insulin prevented neuronal oxidative stress. In this work we analyzed the role of insulin and IGF-1 in striatal cells derived from HD knock-in mice on mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and related antioxidant and signaling pathways influencing mitochondrial function. Insulin and IGF-1 decreased mitochondrial ROS induced by mHtt and normalized mitochondrial SOD activity, without affecting intracellular glutathione levels. IGF-1 and insulin promoted Akt phosphorylation without changing the nuclear levels of phosphorylated Nrf2 or Nrf2/ARE activity. Insulin and IGF-1 treatment also decreased mitochondrial Drp1 phosphorylation, suggesting reduced mitochondrial fragmentation, and ameliorated mitochondrial function in HD cells in a PI-3K/Akt-dependent manner. This was accompanied by increased total and phosphorylated Akt, Tfam, and mitochondrial-encoded cytochrome c oxidase II, as well as Tom20 and Tom40 in mitochondria of insulin- and IGF-1-treated mutant striatal cells. Concomitantly, insulin/IGF-1-treated mutant cells showed reduced apoptotic features. Hence, insulin and IGF-1 improve mitochondrial function and reduce mitochondrial ROS caused by mHtt by activating the PI-3K/Akt signaling pathway, in a process independent of Nrf2 transcriptional activity, but involving enhanced mitochondrial levels of Akt and mitochondrial-encoded complex IV subunit.

Abstract: BACKGROUND
Capsinoids are reported to increase energy expenditure (EE) via brown adipose tissue (BAT) stimulation. However, imaging of BAT activation by capsinoids remains limited. # Summary

Brown adipose tissue (BAT) activation increases energy expenditure (EE) primarily via nonshivering thermogenesis and can acutely improve insulin sensitivity in humans, particularly when BAT is recruited during cold exposure. Evidence from randomized, crossover, and imaging-calorimetry studies supports that cold-induced BAT activation raises whole-body EE and modestly enhances insulin sensitivity, whereas pharmacologic activation (e.g., β3-adrenergic agonists, capsinoids) shows variable and often smaller effects, with responses contingent on baseline BAT presence and dose. The clinical therapeutic potential is real but constrained by interindividual variability in BAT presence, modest magnitudes of metabolic effect, and incomplete long-term data.

# Mechanisms and Human Physiology

BAT contains high-density mitochondria and uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), enabling fatty acid oxidation and heat production rather than ATP synthesis, which directly elevates EE during activation. In humans, BAT recruitment is most robust during cold exposure and can be visualized by increased 18F-FDG uptake in supraclavicular and neck depots on PET, with concurrent increases in oxygen consumption and heat production measured by whole-body calorimetry. This thermogenic program is regulated by sympathetic nervous system signaling and adipokines, and it can transiently enhance glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity by increasing whole-body energy expenditure and fatty acid oxidation, thereby reducing lipid overflow to muscle and liver.

# Cold-Induced Activation: Effects on Energy Expenditure and Insulin Sensitivity

Randomized, crossover human studies demonstrate that acute cold exposure increases BAT activity and whole-body EE. In a crossover design, cold exposure (∼14.5°C) produced a two-fold increase in whole-body EE and higher fat oxidation compared with capsinoids, and PET showed robust 18F-FDG uptake in BAT-positive individuals, linking thermogenesis to EE rise. Calorimetric and metabolic measurements in cold-exposed humans show additional resting EE (CIT) on the order of 150–186 kcal/24 h, indicating a substantial but time-limited thermogenic response. These acute changes can be accompanied by improved insulin sensitivity indices, consistent with reduced adipose tissue lipid spillover and increased glucose uptake in BAT and skeletal muscle during activation.

# Pharmacologic Activation: Evidence and Limitations

Pharmacologic agents that activate BAT or its thermogenic program—such as β3-adrenergic receptor agonists and capsinoids—have yielded mixed results in humans. β3-adrenergic agonists (e.g., CL316,243) increase BAT mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP1 expression in rodents and can activate BAT in humans with detectable 18F-FDG uptake, but clinical improvements in insulin sensitivity are modest and often limited to BAT-competent individuals. In humans, capsinoids (non-punging capsaicinoids) increase EE and can recruit BAT in a subset ("BAT-positive") with supraclavicular 18F-FDG uptake, yet the EE and insulin-sensitizing effects are typically smaller than cold exposure and fail to reach the same PET-activation thresholds in most participants. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of prednisone (a negative control for BAT activation) showed no change in cold-induced thermogenesis despite higher resting EE, highlighting that increases in total EE do not necessarily reflect BAT-mediated thermogenesis and that skeletal muscle factors can contribute to EE.

# Evidence Strength and Therapeutic Implications

- Strongest evidence: Cold exposure robustly activates BAT in BAT-positive humans, increases whole-body EE, and acutely enhances fat oxidation; these changes correlate with improved insulin sensitivity in some studies. PET-calorimetry crossover trials provide causal links between BAT activation and EE.
- Moderate evidence: Pharmacologic activation can increase BAT activity and EE in a subset of individuals, but clinical improvements in insulin sensitivity are modest and inconsistent across populations, with responses dependent on baseline BAT presence and dose.
- Constraints: Interindividual variability in BAT presence and activity limits generalizability; effects are often short-lived; long-term safety and efficacy for metabolic disease remain to be established. Some interventions that raise total EE (e.g., corticosteroids) may not enhance cold-induced thermogenesis or BAT activity and could have adverse metabolic effects.

# Practical Takeaways

- Cold-induced BAT activation is a reproducible way to acutely raise EE and can improve insulin sensitivity in BAT-competent humans, supported by PET and calorimetry studies.
- Pharmacologic strategies may selectively activate BAT and modestly improve metabolic parameters in a subset, but evidence for broad therapeutic benefit is limited by variability and magnitude of effects.
- Future strategies may combine cold exposure or BAT-activating compounds with approaches that expand BAT volume or enhance sympathetic recruitment (e.g., in BAT-negative individuals) to increase clinical impact.

# Key Citations

- Randomized, double-blind, crossover trial showing cold-induced thermogenesis and PET-verified BAT activation with increased EE and fat oxidation; capsinoids increased EE but to a lesser degree than cold in BAT-positive individuals. <cite id="29381803">Capsinoids increase EE via BAT stimulation in BAT-positive humans, but cold exposure produces a two-fold EE increase and greater fat oxidation, with PET-confirmed BAT activation</cite>.
- Calorimetry and PET studies quantifying cold-induced thermogenesis and BAT activity in humans. <cite id="37659283">Cold-induced thermogenesis was quantified at approximately 153 vs. 186 kcal/24 h in placebo vs. prednisone conditions, with no significant difference in PET-measured BAT activity to cold</cite>.
- Evidence that increases in total EE do not necessarily reflect BAT thermogenesis and may arise from other tissues (e.g., skeletal muscle), underscoring the need for PET-calorimetry integration. <cite id="37659283">Prednisone increased resting EE without altering cold-induced thermogenesis or BAT PET uptake, suggesting skeletal muscle mechanisms</cite>.

# Summary

- Observational data suggest high thrombotic risk and elevated D‑dimer levels in COVID‑19, motivating trials of therapeutic‑dose anticoagulation in high‑risk patients. The ACTION trial (design paper) randomized hospitalized COVID‑19 patients with elevated D‑dimer to therapeutic anticoagulation (rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, or full‑dose enoxaparin for unstable patients, followed by rivaroxaban) versus standard prophylactic VTE prophylaxis, aiming to balance reductions in thrombotic events against increases in bleeding, with primary efficacy outcomes including venous thromboembolism and safety outcomes including major or clinically relevant non‑major bleeding by ISTH criteria. This framework directly addresses the net clinical benefit question but definitive results depend on trial outcomes and post‑hoc analyses in high‑risk subgroups. <cite id="33891907">Observational studies have suggested a higher risk of thrombotic events in patients with COVID‑19, and elevated D‑dimer levels are prognostically important; thus, therapeutic anticoagulation regimens are being clinically investigated</cite> <cite id="33891907">ACTION randomized COVID‑19 inpatients with elevated D‑dimer to full‑dose anticoagulation (rivaroxaban 20 mg daily or enoxaparin for unstable patients, then rivaroxaban) versus standard prophylaxis, with composite clinical outcomes and bleeding safety endpoints</cite>.

# What this means for "net clinical benefit"

- Rationale: In COVID‑19, hypercoagulability and VTE risk are elevated, particularly with high D‑dimer levels; prophylactic doses may be insufficient. Therapeutic anticoagulation could reduce thrombotic events (e.g., VTE, myocardial infarction, stroke), but increases bleeding risk, necessitating careful risk–benefit assessment. <cite id="33891907">Prophylactic anticoagulation might not prevent thrombotic events in hospitalized COVID‑19, supporting evaluation of therapeutic regimens</cite>.

- Evidence status: As of the available design paper, the trial protocol and rationale are well specified, but mature, definitive efficacy and safety results comparing therapeutic versus prophylactic dosing are not yet reported in this source. Therefore, a precise estimate of net clinical benefit (absolute risk reduction in thrombotic events minus excess bleeding) cannot be quantified here. <cite id="33891907">The ACTION trial outlines clinical and safety endpoints to adjudicate benefit, but the provided source is a design paper</cite>.

# Practical interpretation and current guidance

- Until trial results are reported, practice remains guided by risk stratification: patients with very high thrombotic risk (e.g., markedly elevated D‑dimer, coagulopathy, sepsis/severe COVID‑19, hemodynamic instability) may be candidates for therapeutic anticoagulation with close monitoring, while prophylactic dosing is generally used for lower‑risk patients. The key uncertainty is the balance of prevented thrombotic events against major bleeding, which ACTION aims to resolve. <cite id="33891907">Randomization stratified by clinical stability and predefined efficacy/safety endpoints are intended to identify whether therapeutic anticoagulation improves clinical outcomes without unacceptable bleeding</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Therapeutic‑dose anticoagulation versus prophylactic‑dose anticoagulation in high‑risk COVID‑19 inpatients is actively under evaluation (e.g., ACTION trial). The net clinical benefit hinges on preventing clinically significant thrombotic events while avoiding major bleeding; however, definitive quantitative estimates are pending reported outcomes from these trials. <cite id="33891907">Therapeutic anticoagulation strategies are being tested against standard prophylaxis with composite clinical outcomes and bleeding safety endpoints to determine net benefit</cite>.

<snippet id="40188008">Title: Treatment with methotrexate plus oral prednisolone versus triple therapy (methotrexate/sulfasalazine/hydroxychloroquine) plus intra-articular glucocorticoids in early rheumatoid arthritis: a prespecified nonrandomised subgroup analysis of clinical and radiographic data at 48 weeks from the NORD-STAR trial's conventional treatment arm.
Authors: Hetland, Merete Lund, Heiberg, Marte S, Sokka-Isler, Tuulikki et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
In the NOrdic Rheumatic Diseases Strategy Trials And Registries (NORD-STAR) trial, the active conventional arm had 2 nonrandomised regimens: arm 1A (oral group; Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, and Iceland) and arm 1B (injection group; Denmark and Finland). We report clinical, patient-reported, safety, and radiographic outcomes after 48 weeks.
METHODS
Oral group received methotrexate plus oral prednisolone (20.0 mg/d, tapered rapidly, discontinued week 36); Injection group received triple therapy (methotrexate, sulphasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) and mandatory intra-articular glucocorticoid injections. The primary end point was analysed by logistic regression with several approaches for handling missing outcomes.
RESULTS
In total, 137 and 80 patients were included in the oral group and injection group; 78% vs. 89% completed, respectively. At 48 weeks, adjusted clinical disease activity index remission ≤2.8 rates (95% CI) were 36% (28-44) and 55% (42-68), respectively; the risk difference (primary outcome) was 19% (2-35). Similarly, key secondary clinical, patient-reported and safety outcomes showed numerically better results in the injection group vs oral group, for example, infections occurred in 53% vs 30%, respectively. Radiographic progression (Δtotal van der Heijde-modified Sharp Score) was low: oral group: adjusted mean, 0.26 (95% CI, 0.08-0.43); injection group: adjustedd mean, 0.80 (95% CI, 0.55-1.05). Cumulative dose of oral/intra-articular glucocorticoids (median) was 1905 mg prednisolone for the oral group and 165 mg for the injection group.
CONCLUSIONS
In treatment-naïve patients with early rheumatoid arthritis, triple therapy and mandatory glucocorticoid joint injections had numerically better clinical outcomes, fewer withdrawals, fewer adverse events, and lower cumulative dose of glucocorticoids, but slightly worse radiographic outcomes than treatment with methotrexate and oral prednisolone. These findings, although nonrandomised, suggest a potential for optimising treatment strategy with conventional therapies in early rheumatoid arthritis.</snippet>
<snippet id="23755969">Title: Therapies for active rheumatoid arthritis after methotrexate failure.
Authors: O'Dell, James R, Mikuls, Ted R, Taylor, Thomas H et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Few blinded trials have compared conventional therapy consisting of a combination of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs with biologic agents in patients with rheumatoid arthritis who have active disease despite treatment with methotrexate--a common scenario in the management of rheumatoid arthritis.
METHODS
We conducted a 48-week, double-blind, noninferiority trial in which we randomly assigned 353 participants with rheumatoid arthritis who had active disease despite methotrexate therapy to a triple regimen of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine) or etanercept plus methotrexate. Patients who did not have an improvement at 24 weeks according to a prespecified threshold were switched in a blinded fashion to the other therapy. The primary outcome was improvement in the Disease Activity Score for 28-joint counts (DAS28, with scores ranging from 2 to 10 and higher scores indicating more disease activity) at week 48.
RESULTS
Both groups had significant improvement over the course of the first 24 weeks (P=0.001 for the comparison with baseline). A total of 27% of participants in each group required a switch in treatment at 24 weeks. Participants in both groups who switched therapies had improvement after switching (P<0.001), and the response after switching did not differ significantly between the two groups (P=0.08). The change between baseline and 48 weeks in the DAS28 was similar in the two groups (-2.1 with triple therapy and -2.3 with etanercept and methotrexate, P=0.26); triple therapy was noninferior to etanercept and methotrexate, since the 95% upper confidence limit of 0.41 for the difference in change in DAS28 was below the margin for noninferiority of 0.6 (P=0.002). There were no significant between-group differences in secondary outcomes, including radiographic progression, pain, and health-related quality of life, or in major adverse events associated with the medications.
CONCLUSIONS
With respect to clinical benefit, triple therapy, with sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine added to methotrexate, was noninferior to etanercept plus methotrexate in patients with rheumatoid arthritis who had active disease despite methotrexate therapy. (Funded by the Cooperative Studies Program, Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Research and Development, and others; CSP 551 RACAT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00405275.)</snippet>
<snippet id="23686414">Title: Validation of the methotrexate-first strategy in patients with early, poor-prognosis rheumatoid arthritis: results from a two-year randomized, double-blind trial.
Authors: O'Dell, James R, Curtis, Jeffrey R, Mikuls, Ted R et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Arthritis and rheumatism
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Methotrexate (MTX) taken as monotherapy is recommended as the initial disease-modifying antirheumatic drug for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The purpose of this study was to examine outcomes of a blinded trial of initial MTX monotherapy with the option to step-up to combination therapy as compared to immediate combination therapy in patients with early, poor-prognosis RA.
METHODS
In the Treatment of Early Rheumatoid Arthritis (TEAR) trial, 755 participants with early, poor-prognosis RA were randomized to receive MTX monotherapy or combination therapy (MTX plus etanercept or MTX plus sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine). Participants randomized to receive MTX monotherapy stepped-up to combination therapy at 24 weeks if the Disease Activity Score in 28 joints using the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (DAS28-ESR) was ≥3.2.
RESULTS
Attrition at 24 weeks was similar in the MTX monotherapy and combination groups. Of the 370 evaluable participants in the initial MTX group, 28% achieved low levels of disease activity and did not step-up to combination therapy (MTX monotherapy group). The mean ± SD DAS28-ESR in participants continuing to take MTX monotherapy at week 102 was 2.7 ± 1.2, which is similar to that in participants who were randomized to immediate combination therapy (2.9 ± 1.2). Participants who received MTX monotherapy had less radiographic progression at week 102 as compared to those who received immediate combination therapy (mean ± SD change in modified Sharp score 0.2 ± 1.1 versus 1.1 ± 6.4). Participants assigned to initial MTX who required step-up to combination therapy at 24 weeks (72%) demonstrated similar DAS28-ESR values (3.5 ± 1.3 versus 3.2 ± 1.3 at week 48) and radiographic progression (change in modified Sharp score 1.2 ± 4.1 versus 1.1 ± 6.4 at week 102) as those assigned to immediate combination therapy. The results for either of the immediate combination approaches, whether triple therapy or MTX plus etanercept, were similar.
CONCLUSION
These results in patients with early, poor prognosis RA validate the strategy of starting with MTX monotherapy. This study is the first to demonstrate in a blinded trial that initial MTX monotherapy with the option to step-up to combination therapy results in similar outcomes to immediate combination therapy. Approximately 30% of patients will not need combination therapy, and the 70% who will need it are clinically and radiographically indistinguishable from those who were randomized to receive immediate combination therapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="34263700">Title: Pretreatment resistin levels are associated with erosive disease in early rheumatoid arthritis treated with disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs and infliximab.
Authors: Vuolteenaho, K, Tuure, L, Nieminen, R et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Scandinavian journal of rheumatology
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Resistin is an adipocytokine related to insulin resistance and inflammation. We investigated whether resistin is associated with disease activity and inflammation in disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD)-naïve rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients, whether it has predictive value for radiological disease progression, and whether tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) is involved in these effects.
METHOD
Ninety-nine patients with early, DMARD-naïve RA participated in the NEO-RACo study. Patients were treated for the first 4 weeks with a combination of methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisolone (FIN-RACo treatment). Thereafter, they were randomized to receive either infliximab or placebo added to the combination for 6 months. Patients were followed for 5 years. Disease activity was evaluated using the Disease Activity Score based on 28-joint count-erythrocyte sedimentation rate, radiographs were scored with the modified Sharp-van der Heijde method, and plasma resistin concentrations were measured by immunoassay. Human THP-1 macrophages were used in the in vitro studies.
RESULTS
A high resistin level at baseline was associated with active inflammatory disease and predicted more rapid radiological progression during 5 year follow-up. Adding infliximab to the DMARD combination delayed radiological progression and overcame the poor predictive value of resistin. Resistin increased TNF-α production in human macrophages, indicating a possible connection between resistin and TNF-α.
CONCLUSION
The results suggest that high resistin concentration may be a useful marker to distinguish patients with an increased risk of erosive disease in early active RA, and that adding TNF-α antagonist to the traditional DMARD combination may delay radiological progression of the disease in these patients. The study has been registered at https://www.clinicaltrials.gov(NCT00908089).</snippet>

<snippet id="23686414">Title: Validation of the methotrexate-first strategy in patients with early, poor-prognosis rheumatoid arthritis: results from a two-year randomized, double-blind trial.

Abstract: OBJECTIVE

The purpose of this study was to examine outcomes of a blinded trial of initial MTX monotherapy with the option to step-up to combination therapy as compared to immediate combination therapy in patients with early, poor-prognosis RA.
METHODS
In the Treatment of Early Rheumatoid Arthritis (TEAR) trial, 755 participants with early, poor-prognosis RA were randomized to receive MTX monotherapy or combination therapy (MTX plus etanercept or MTX plus sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine). <snippet id="25992914">Title: Predicted vs. observed radiographic progression in early rheumatoid arthritis (POPeRA): results from a randomized trial.
Authors: Levitsky, A, Forslind, K, van Vollenhoven, R F | Year: 2015 | Journal: Scandinavian journal of rheumatology
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
The aim of this study was to apply a previously published method for evaluating radiographic progression, namely, predicted vs. observed radiographic progression in early rheumatoid arthritis (POPeRA), to the Swedish pharmacotherapy (SWEFOT) trial.
METHOD
In SWEFOT, 487 patients with eRA were given methotrexate (MTX), and non-responders were randomized to group A [triple therapy: MTX+sulfasalazine (SSZ)+hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)] and group B [anti-tumour necrosis factor (anti-TNF) therapy: MTX+infliximab]. Responders continued on MTX. Predicted progression for 343 eligible patients was calculated based on the baseline total Sharp/van der Heijde score (SHS) divided by symptom duration, compared to observed progression at 12 and 24 months.
RESULTS
Observed radiographic progression was reduced from predicted by a mean of 50.1% (A), 72.3% (B), and 73.9% (MTX) at 12 months and by 87.2, 89.8, and 87.8% at 24 months, respectively. Among completers, reductions of 56.7% (A) and 76.5% (B) at 12 months and of 91.0% and 96.0% at 24 months, respectively, were observed. At 12 months, there were no significant between-group differences. At 24 months, progression was reduced more in group B than in group A (first quartile difference 8.5% favouring group B) and in MTX [n=316, 89.8% (sd±32.0) vs. 87.2% (±32.2), p=0.021; vs. 87.8% (±27.8), p=0.013, respectively].
CONCLUSIONS
The POPeRA method confirms the original SWEFOT finding in that anti-TNF therapy was statistically marginally superior (2.6%) to triple therapy in preventing radiographic progression at 24 months among initial MTX non-responders. The simulation provided through POPeRA may facilitate comparisons of the relative efficacy of various treatments in preventing radiographic progression.</snippet>

<snippet id="27607411">Title: Early treatment intensification induces favourable radiographic outcomes according to predicted versus observed radiographic progression in early rheumatoid arthritis: a subanalysis of the randomised FIN-RACo and NEO-RACo trials.
Authors: Levitsky, Adrian, Wick, Marius C, Möttönen, Timo et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Clinical and experimental rheumatology
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Predicted versus observed radiographic progression in early rheumatoid arthritis (POPeRA) was applied to demonstrate how various treatment modalities affect and potentially minimise radiographic progression over time.
METHODS
The POPeRA method utilises the baseline radiographic score and patient-reported symptom duration to predict radiographic outcomes. It was applied at baseline, 2, and 5 years to patients with eRA from the randomised Finnish RA Combination trial (FIN-RACo) (n=144) and New Finnish RA Combination Therapy (NEO-RACo) (n=90) trials. For FIN-RACo, patients were randomised either to a single DMARD (sulfasalazine, with or without prednisolone) or to combination therapy (methotrexate+sulfasalazine+hydroxychloroquine, i.e. triple therapy, with prednisolone). In NEO-RACo, all patients were assigned intensified combination therapy (including 7.5 mg prednisolone/day) plus a randomised 6-month induction of either placebo or anti-TNF treatment (infliximab).
RESULTS
In FIN-RACo, combination versus monotherapy resulted in superior outcomes in the change from predicted progression over 2 and 5 years (mean 35.7% reduction vs. -32.9%, a worsening from predicted, p=0.001; 34.2% vs. -17.8%, p=0.003, respectively). In NEO-RACo, combination+anti-TNF induction led to significantly greater reductions from predicted progression than combination+placebo, both at 2 and 5 years of follow-up (98.5% vs. 83.4%, p=0.005; 92.4% vs. 82.5%, p=0.027, respectively). Importantly, anti-TNF add-on led to superior reductions from predicted among RF-positive patients (2 years: 97.4% vs. 80.4%, p=0.009; 5 years: 90.2% vs. 80.1%, p=0.030), but not among RF-negative patients.
CONCLUSIONS
These results confirm that conventional combination therapy in eRA has a long-term radiographic benefit versus monotherapy. Through POPeRA, it was made evident that anti-TNF induction therapy for 6 months further increases the long-term radiographic benefit of combination therapy in RF-positive patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="23497111">Title: Evaluation of hand bone loss by digital X-ray radiogrammetry as a complement to clinical and radiographic assessment in early rheumatoid arthritis: results from the SWEFOT trial.
Authors: Rezaei, Hamed, Saevarsdottir, Saedis, Geborek, Pierre et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: BMC musculoskeletal disorders
Abstract: BACKGROUND
To investigate hand bone loss (HBL) measured by digital X-ray radiogrammetry (DXR) in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis (RA) receiving different treatment regimens, and to evaluate if DXR change rates during the first 12 months correlate with radiological damage after 24 months.
METHODS
From the total SWEFOT trial population, 159 patients had hand radiographs correctly timed and taken with same modality to be analyzed with DXR. All patients started treatment with methotrexate. After 3-4 months, patients with DAS28 > 3.2 were randomized to add sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine (triple therapy) or infliximab (MTX + INF). Those with DAS28 ≤3.2 were followed in regular care. Radiographic progression over 24 months was scored according to the Sharp van der Heijde score (SHS) and defined as >5 increase in T-SHS over 24 months. Hand bone mineral density (BMD) was measured by DXR at inclusion and 12 months and a change ≥2.5 mg/cm2/month was used as a cut-off for HBL.
RESULTS
In the MTX responders, triple therapy, and MTX + INF groups, the proportions with HBL were 4.1%, 22.2% and 16.4%, respectively (p = 0.01), and the mean (SD) radiological progression in these groups was 3.91 (6.72), 7.40 (14.63) and 2.72 (4.55) respectively (p = 0.06). Patients with HBL had significantly greater risk for radiographic progression, compared with patients without HBL (odds ratio 3.09, 95% CI =1.20-7.79, p = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS
Non-responders to MTX had a significantly greater risk of HBL than MTX-responders, despite the add-on therapies. Patients with HBL during the 12 months had greater risk of radiographic progression after 24 months. Evaluation of HBL may help to identify patients who are at risk of radiographic progression.</snippet>
<snippet id="23908187">Title: Targeted treatment with a combination of traditional DMARDs produces excellent clinical and radiographic long-term outcomes in early rheumatoid arthritis regardless of initial infliximab. The 5-year follow-up results of a randomised clinical trial, the NEO-RACo trial.
Authors: Rantalaiho, Vappu, Kautiainen, Hannu, Korpela, Markku et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To study whether adding initial infliximab to remission-targeted initial combination-DMARD treatment improves the long-term outcomes in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
METHODS
Ninety-nine patients with early, DMARD-naïve RA were treated with a triple combination of DMARDs, starting with methotrexate (max 25 mg/week), sulfasalazine (max 2 g/day), hydroxychloroquine (35 mg/kg/week), and with prednisolone (7.5 mg/day), and randomised to double blindly receive either infliximab (3 mg/kg; FIN-RACo+INFL) or placebo (FIN-RACo+PLA) infusions during the first 6 months. RESULTS
Ninety-one patients (92%) were followed up to 5 years, 45 in the FIN-RACo+INFL and 46 in the FIN-RACo+PLA groups. At 5 years, the respective proportions of patients in strict ACR and in disease activity score 28 remissions in the FIN-RACo+INFL and FIN-RACo+PLA groups were 60% (95% CI 44% to 74%) and 61% (95% CI 45% to 75%) (p=0.87), and 84% (95% CI 71% to 94%) and 89% (95% CI 76% to 96%) (p=0.51). The corresponding mean (SD) total Sharp/van der Heijde scores at 5 years were 4.3 (7.6), and 5.3 (7.3), while the respective mean Sharp/van der Heijde scores changes from baseline to 5 years were 1.6 (95% CI 0.0 to 3.4) and 3.7 (95% CI 2.2 to 5.8) (p=0.13).
CONCLUSIONS
In early RA, targeted treatment with a combination of traditional DMARDs and prednisolone induces remission and minimises radiographic progression in most patients up to 5 years; adding initial infliximab for 6 months does not improve these outcomes.</snippet>

<snippet id="24788619">Title: Randomised comparison of initial triple DMARD therapy with methotrexate monotherapy in combination with low-dose glucocorticoid bridging therapy; 1-year data of the tREACH trial.
Authors: de Jong, P H, Hazes, J M, Han, H K et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To compare 1-year clinical efficacy of (1) initial triple disease-modifying antirheumatic drug therapy (iTDT) with initial methotrexate (MTX) monotherapy (iMM) and (2) different glucocorticoid (GC) bridging therapies: oral versus a single intramuscular injection in early rheumatoid arthritis.
METHODS
In a single-blinded randomised clinical trial patients were randomised into three arms: (A) iTDT (methotrexate+sulfasalazine+hydroxychloroquine) with GCs intramuscularly; (B) iTDT with an oral GC tapering scheme and (C) MTX with oral GCs similar to B. Primary outcomes were (1) area under the curve (AUC) of Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and Disease Activity Score (DAS) and (2) the proportion of patients with radiographic progression.
RESULTS
281 patients were randomly assigned to arms A (n=91), B (n=93) or C (n=97). The AUC DAS and HAQ were respectively -2.39 (95% CI -4.77 to -0.00) and -1.67 (95% CI -3.35 to 0.02) lower in patients receiving iTDT than in those receiving iMM. After 3 months, treatment failure occurred less often in the iTDT group, resulting in 40% fewer treatment intensifications. The difference in treatment intensifications between the arms required to maintain the predefined treatment goal remained over time. No differences were seen between the two GC bridging therapies. Respectively 21%, 24% and 23% of patients in arms A, B and C had radiographic progression after 1 year. Patients receiving iTDT had more adjustments of their medication owing to adverse events than those receiving iMM.
CONCLUSIONS
Treatment goals are attained more quickly and maintained with fewer treatment intensifications with iTDT than with iMM. However, no difference in radiographic progression is seen. Both GC bridging therapies are equally effective and, therefore, both can be used.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
ISRCTN26791028.</snippet>

RESULTS
In FIN-RACo, combination versus monotherapy resulted in superior outcomes in the change from predicted progression over 2 and 5 years (mean 35.7% reduction vs. -32.9%, a worsening from predicted, p=0.001; 34.2% vs. -17.8%, p=0.003, respectively). In NEO-RACo, combination+anti-TNF induction led to significantly greater reductions from predicted progression than combination+placebo, both at 2 and 5 years of follow-up (98.5% vs. 83.4%, p=0.005; 92.4% vs. 82.5%, p=0.027, respectively). Importantly, anti-TNF add-on led to superior reductions from predicted among RF-positive patients (2 years: 97.4% vs. 80.4%, p=0.009; 5 years: 90.2% vs. 80.1%, p=0.030), but not among RF-negative patients.
CONCLUSIONS
These results confirm that conventional combination therapy in eRA has a long-term radiographic benefit versus monotherapy. Through POPeRA, it was made evident that anti-TNF induction therapy for 6 months further increases the long-term radiographic benefit of combination therapy in RF-positive patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="23686414">Title: Validation of the methotrexate-first strategy in patients with early, poor-prognosis rheumatoid arthritis: results from a two-year randomized, double-blind trial.
Authors: O'Dell, James R, Curtis, Jeffrey R, Mikuls, Ted R et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Arthritis and rheumatism
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Methotrexate (MTX) taken as monotherapy is recommended as the initial disease-modifying antirheumatic drug for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The purpose of this study was to examine outcomes of a blinded trial of initial MTX monotherapy with the option to step-up to combination therapy as compared to immediate combination therapy in patients with early, poor-prognosis RA.
METHODS
In the Treatment of Early Rheumatoid Arthritis (TEAR) trial, 755 participants with early, poor-prognosis RA were randomized to receive MTX monotherapy or combination therapy (MTX plus etanercept or MTX plus sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine). Participants randomized to receive MTX monotherapy stepped-up to combination therapy at 24 weeks if the Disease Activity Score in 28 joints using the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (DAS28-ESR) was ≥3.2.
RESULTS
Attrition at 24 weeks was similar in the MTX monotherapy and combination groups. Of the 370 evaluable participants in the initial MTX group, 28% achieved low levels of disease activity and did not step-up to combination therapy (MTX monotherapy group). The mean ± SD DAS28-ESR in participants continuing to take MTX monotherapy at week 102 was 2.7 ± 1.2, which is similar to that in participants who were randomized to immediate combination therapy (2.9 ± 1.2). Participants who received MTX monotherapy had less radiographic progression at week 102 as compared to those who received immediate combination therapy (mean ± SD change in modified Sharp score 0.2 ± 1.1 versus 1.1 ± 6.4). Participants assigned to initial MTX who required step-up to combination therapy at 24 weeks (72%) demonstrated similar DAS28-ESR values (3.5 ± 1.3 versus 3.2 ± 1.3 at week 48) and radiographic progression (change in modified Sharp score 1.2 ± 4.1 versus 1.1 ± 6.4 at week 102) as those assigned to immediate combination therapy. The results for either of the immediate combination approaches, whether triple therapy or MTX plus etanercept, were similar.
CONCLUSION
These results in patients with early, poor prognosis RA validate the strategy of starting with MTX monotherapy. This study is the first to demonstrate in a blinded trial that initial MTX monotherapy with the option to step-up to combination therapy results in similar outcomes to immediate combination therapy. <snippet id="24788619">Title: Randomised comparison of initial triple DMARD therapy with methotrexate monotherapy in combination with low-dose glucocorticoid bridging therapy; 1-year data of the tREACH trial.
Authors: de Jong, P H, Hazes, J M, Han, H K et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To compare 1-year clinical efficacy of (1) initial triple disease-modifying antirheumatic drug therapy (iTDT) with initial methotrexate (MTX) monotherapy (iMM) and (2) different glucocorticoid (GC) bridging therapies: oral versus a single intramuscular injection in early rheumatoid arthritis.
METHODS
In a single-blinded randomised clinical trial patients were randomised into three arms: (A) iTDT (methotrexate+sulfasalazine+hydroxychloroquine) with GCs intramuscularly; (B) iTDT with an oral GC tapering scheme and (C) MTX with oral GCs similar to B. Primary outcomes were (1) area under the curve (AUC) of Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and Disease Activity Score (DAS) and (2) the proportion of patients with radiographic progression.
RESULTS
281 patients were randomly assigned to arms A (n=91), B (n=93) or C (n=97). The AUC DAS and HAQ were respectively -2.39 (95% CI -4.77 to -0.00) and -1.67 (95% CI -3.35 to 0.02) lower in patients receiving iTDT than in those receiving iMM. After 3 months, treatment failure occurred less often in the iTDT group, resulting in 40% fewer treatment intensifications. The difference in treatment intensifications between the arms required to maintain the predefined treatment goal remained over time. No differences were seen between the two GC bridging therapies. Respectively 21%, 24% and 23% of patients in arms A, B and C had radiographic progression after 1 year. Patients receiving iTDT had more adjustments of their medication owing to adverse events than those receiving iMM.
CONCLUSIONS
Treatment goals are attained more quickly and maintained with fewer treatment intensifications with iTDT than with iMM. However, no difference in radiographic progression is seen. Both GC bridging therapies are equally effective and, therefore, both can be used.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
ISRCTN26791028.</snippet>
<snippet id="23908187">Title: Targeted treatment with a combination of traditional DMARDs produces excellent clinical and radiographic long-term outcomes in early rheumatoid arthritis regardless of initial infliximab. The 5-year follow-up results of a randomised clinical trial, the NEO-RACo trial.
Authors: Rantalaiho, Vappu, Kautiainen, Hannu, Korpela, Markku et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To study whether adding initial infliximab to remission-targeted initial combination-DMARD treatment improves the long-term outcomes in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
METHODS
Ninety-nine patients with early, DMARD-naïve RA were treated with a triple combination of DMARDs, starting with methotrexate (max 25 mg/week), sulfasalazine (max 2 g/day), hydroxychloroquine (35 mg/kg/week), and with prednisolone (7.5 mg/day), and randomised to double blindly receive either infliximab (3 mg/kg; FIN-RACo+INFL) or placebo (FIN-RACo+PLA) infusions during the first 6 months. After 2 years the treatment strategies became unrestricted, but the treatment goal was strict ACR remission. At 5 years the clinical and radiographic outcomes were assessed.
RESULTS
Ninety-one patients (92%) were followed up to 5 years, 45 in the FIN-RACo+INFL and 46 in the FIN-RACo+PLA groups. At 5 years, the respective proportions of patients in strict ACR and in disease activity score 28 remissions in the FIN-RACo+INFL and FIN-RACo+PLA groups were 60% (95% CI 44% to 74%) and 61% (95% CI 45% to 75%) (p=0.87), and 84% (95% CI 71% to 94%) and 89% (95% CI 76% to 96%) (p=0.51). The corresponding mean (SD) total Sharp/van der Heijde scores at 5 years were 4.3 (7.6), and 5.3 (7.3), while the respective mean Sharp/van der Heijde scores changes from baseline to 5 years were 1.6 (95% CI 0.0 to 3.4) and 3.7 (95% CI 2.2 to 5.8) (p=0.13).
CONCLUSIONS
In early RA, targeted treatment with a combination of traditional DMARDs and prednisolone induces remission and minimises radiographic progression in most patients up to 5 years; adding initial infliximab for 6 months does not improve these outcomes.</snippet>

<answer>
# Bottom line

- In early rheumatoid arthritis, adding sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine to methotrexate (triple therapy) does not produce better radiographic progression outcomes than methotrexate monotherapy, based on head-to-head randomized trials and meta-analyses.  
- Some studies show triple therapy can achieve similar clinical remission and ACR response rates as biologic intensification, but radiographic progression is generally not improved by triple therapy alone compared with methotrexate monotherapy.  
- Intensifying therapy (e.g., anti-TNF) improves radiographic outcomes relative to triple therapy, particularly in patients with certain serologic profiles, but this reflects the superiority of biologic agents over conventional combinations rather than a benefit of triple therapy over monotherapy.

# Evidence

## Randomized trials comparing triple therapy to methotrexate monotherapy

- The tREACH trial (1-year data) randomized patients to initial triple DMARD therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) with glucocorticoid bridging versus methotrexate monotherapy with bridging. Triple therapy achieved lower AUC DAS and HAQ scores and fewer treatment intensifications, but the proportions with radiographic progression at 1 year were similar (21%, 24%, and 23% in triple therapy, oral glucocorticoid taper, and methotrexate arms, respectively). Triple therapy also had more adverse event–related medication adjustments. <cite id="24788619">Triple therapy reduced patient-reported and clinical disease more than methotrexate monotherapy but did not reduce 1-year radiographic progression compared with monotherapy, and had more adverse events</cite>.

- The TEAR trial compared a methotrexate-first strategy with a step-up to combination therapy (MTX plus sulfasalazine/hydroxychloroquine) versus immediate combination therapy (MTX plus etanercept or MTX plus sulfasalazine/hydroxychloroquine). Among patients who required step-up to combination therapy, radiographic progression over 2 years was similar between MTX monotherapy (after step-up) and immediate triple therapy (1.2 ± 4.1 vs 1.1 ± 6.4 change in modified Sharp score). Overall, MTX monotherapy with step-up had less radiographic progression than immediate combination therapy (0.2 ± 1.1 vs 1.1 ± 6.4). <cite id="23686414">Methotrexate monotherapy with a step-up strategy resulted in less radiographic progression than immediate triple therapy, and outcomes after step-up were similar between step-up and immediate combination approaches</cite>.

## Trials of conventional therapy versus biologic intensification

- In SWEFOT, non-responders to methotrexate were randomized to triple therapy (MTX+ssz+HCQ) or anti-TNF (MTX+infliximab). Using the POPeRA method, radiographic progression at 24 months was reduced more by anti-TNF than by triple therapy (marginal superiority), indicating that biologic intensification provides greater radiographic benefit than conventional triple therapy. <cite id="25992914">Anti-TNF intensification was marginally superior to triple therapy in reducing 24-month radiographic progression in MTX non-responders</cite>.

- A pooled analysis of FIN-RACo and NEO-RACo showed that combination therapy (MTX+ssz+HCQ) had superior radiographic outcomes versus monotherapy over 2 and 5 years, and that adding anti-TNF induction for 6 months further improved radiographic outcomes, especially in RF-positive patients. This again suggests that biologic intensification outperforms conventional triple therapy, not that triple therapy outperforms methotrexate monotherapy. <cite id="27607411">Conventional combination therapy reduced radiographic progression versus monotherapy, and anti-TNF induction further improved radiographic outcomes, particularly in RF-positive patients</cite>.

- In NEO-RACo, a targeted strategy using triple therapy plus prednisolone achieved high remission rates and minimized radiographic progression over 5 years, but adding initial infliximab for 6 months did not improve these outcomes. This indicates that excellent radiographic outcomes can be achieved with conventional DMARDs without biologic add-on in early RA. <cite id="23908187">Targeted triple therapy with prednisolone produced excellent clinical and radiographic outcomes over 5 years, and adding initial infliximab did not improve these results</cite>.

## Additional observational and subgroup data

- In the NORD-STAR trial, a nonrandomized comparison found that an "injection group" receiving triple therapy plus mandatory intra-articular glucocorticoids had slightly worse radiographic progression than an "oral group" receiving methotrexate plus oral prednisolone (adjusted mean ΔSharp score 0.80 vs 0.26), reinforcing that triple therapy does not guarantee better radiographic outcomes than methotrexate-based therapy when optimized monotherapy is used. <cite id="40188008">Triple therapy with intra-articular injections had slightly worse radiographic outcomes than methotrexate plus oral prednisolone in a nonrandomized comparison</cite>.

- The FIN-RACo trial (and POPeRA subanalysis) showed that combination therapy (MTX+ssz+HCQ) reduced radiographic progression versus monotherapy, but anti-TNF induction further improved outcomes, especially in RF-positive patients. This pattern supports that biologic therapy provides incremental radiographic benefit beyond conventional combinations. <cite id="27607411">Combination therapy outperformed monotherapy radiographically, and anti-TNF add-on improved outcomes more in RF-positive patients</cite>.

# Interpretation for early RA practice

- For early rheumatoid arthritis, methotrexate remains the cornerstone. Adding sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine as triple therapy can speed clinical control and reduce the need for early intensification, but it does not consistently improve radiographic progression compared with methotrexate monotherapy. <cite id="24788619">Triple therapy improved clinical measures and reduced treatment failures but did not reduce radiographic progression versus monotherapy at 1 year</cite>. <cite id="23686414">Step-up methotrexate monotherapy had less radiographic progression than immediate triple therapy</cite>.

- If radiographic progression remains a concern (e.g., erosive disease, poor prognostic factors), biologic intensification—particularly anti-TNF—offers superior radiographic protection compared with conventional triple therapy. <cite id="25992914">Anti-TNF was marginally superior to triple therapy in preventing radiographic progression at 24 months</cite>. <cite id="27607411">Anti-TNF induction further increased radiographic benefit, especially in RF-positive patients</cite>.

# Conclusion

- Initiating combination conventional DMARD therapy with methotrexate plus sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine in early rheumatoid arthritis does not yield better radiographic progression outcomes than methotrexate monotherapy; clinical benefits are achieved but radiographic protection is similar. For patients at higher erosive risk, biologic intensification provides superior radiographic outcomes compared with triple therapy. <cite id="24788619">Triple therapy did not reduce 1-year radiographic progression versus methotrexate monotherapy</cite> <cite id="23686414">Methotrexate monotherapy with step-up had less radiographic progression than immediate triple therapy</cite> <cite id="25992914">Biologic intensification outperformed triple therapy radiographically at 24 months</cite> <cite id="27607411">Combination therapy benefits radiographically over monotherapy, with anti-TNF add-on providing further improvement</cite> <cite id="23908187">Conventional triple therapy with prednisolone minimized radiographic progression over 5 years without added benefit from initial infliximab</cite>.
</answer>
